title: Given an unsorted array of numbers and a value K, find the Kth smallest number. Explain how a max-heap of size K keeps the K smallest seen so far, with its root being the answer.
shortTitle: Kth Smallest Number (Find the Kth Smallest with a Max-Heap)

s1_definition.profdef: Kth Smallest Number is a Top K Elements problem solved with a max-heap of size K. We keep the K smallest numbers seen so far in a max-heap, whose root is the largest of those K, which is exactly the Kth smallest overall once all numbers are processed. Each new number replaces the root only if it is smaller, giving O(n log K) time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, to find the Kth cheapest fee among many charged, we keep a small bucket of only the K smallest fees seen, where the biggest of those K sits on top. A new fee enters only if it is smaller than that top one, and after all fees are seen, the top of the bucket is the Kth smallest fee.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a max-heap of size K of the smallest numbers; its root is the Kth smallest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kth Smallest Number is a Top K Elements problem solved with a max-heap of size K. We keep the K smallest numbers seen so far in a max-heap, whose root is the largest of those K, which is exactly the Kth smallest overall once all numbers are processed. Each new number replaces the root only if it is smaller, giving O(n log K) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, to find the Kth cheapest fee among many charged, we keep a small bucket of only the K smallest fees seen, where the biggest of those K sits on top. A new fee enters only if it is smaller than that top one, and after all fees are seen, the top of the bucket is the Kth smallest fee.

**One line to remember:** Keep a max-heap of size K of the smallest numbers; its root is the Kth smallest.

sections.s2_technical:
We use a max-heap, which in Java is `new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder())`. We offer the first K numbers, then for each remaining number, if it is smaller than the root, which is the largest of the kept K, we poll the root and offer the new number. For example, `if (num < maxHeap.peek()) { maxHeap.poll(); maxHeap.offer(num); }`. After processing all numbers, `maxHeap.peek()` is the Kth smallest, because exactly the K smallest numbers remain and the root is the largest of them.

This mirrors Top K Numbers but inverted: there we used a min-heap to keep the K largest; here we use a max-heap to keep the K smallest. The root always being the largest of the kept K is why it equals the Kth smallest at the end.

A senior nuance is that this general heap method handles streaming data where we cannot sort, and it extends to the Kth largest by flipping to a min-heap. For a one-shot in-memory array, quickselect gives average O(n), which is worth mentioning as the alternative when a single query on a static array is all that is needed. Complexity is O(n log K) time and O(K) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants the Kth smallest fee among many charged across accounts, for a fairness audit, without sorting all fees. This is exactly how Kth Smallest Number works.

Problem 2 — Sorting all fees to index the Kth smallest is wasteful. This is why we keep a max-heap of size K holding the K smallest fees, so the root is always the current Kth-smallest candidate and updates cheaply.

The code defines a `FeeAuditService` exposing `kthSmallest(fees, k)` returning the Kth smallest fee. A `Demo` finds the third smallest fee and logs it.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: fees 120, 45, 300, 75, 200, 30, 150 and K equal to 3.

Step 1: Seed the max-heap with 120, 45, 300; the root, the largest, is 300.

Step 2: Next fee 75 is less than root 300, so pop 300 and push 75; the heap holds 120, 45, 75 with root 120.

Step 3: Next fee 200 is not less than root 120, so ignore it. Next fee 30 is less than root 120, so pop 120 and push 30; the heap holds 45, 75, 30 with root 75.

Step 4: Next fee 150 is not less than root 75, so ignore it.

Step 5: The heap holds the three smallest fees 30, 45, 75, and the root 75 is the third smallest fee.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  fees stream, K=3
    │ seed max-heap with first 3 → root = largest kept
    ▼
  for each next fee:
    ├─ fee < root → poll root, offer fee
    └─ else       → discard
    ▼
  heap = {30, 45, 75}; root 75 = 3rd smallest
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kth Smallest Number is a Top K Elements problem, and the heap choice is again the counter-intuitive part: to find the Kth smallest I keep a max-heap of size K. The heap holds the K smallest numbers seen so far, and because it is a max-heap its root is the largest of those K, which once all numbers are processed is precisely the Kth smallest overall.

I seed the heap with the first K numbers, then for every remaining number I compare it against the root. If the new number is smaller than the root, it belongs among the K smallest, so I evict the root and insert it; otherwise I discard it. The root being the largest kept value is what makes the keep-or-discard test a single peek, and it is also why the root is the answer at the end.

At the National Bank of India I used this for a fairness audit that needed the Kth smallest fee among many charged across accounts, without sorting every fee. I kept a size-K max-heap of the smallest fees, where each new fee displaced the largest kept fee only if it was smaller, and read the root as the answer, all in n log K time. I would also mention quickselect as an average linear-time alternative for a single query on a static array, which shows an interviewer I know when the heap is the right tool and when it is not.
